In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 162 times across 17 books, and translators render it "kingdom" in 156 of those cases (100% of the times it gets its own English word), with the other 6 absorbed into phrasing. In the Septuagint it shows up 281 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew words מַמְלָכָה and מַלְכוּת, both of which carry the same blend of "reign" and "realm." The lexicons note an even narrower usage where the word can mean the royal majesty or the king himself, much like calling someone "His Majesty."

prose.def: A royal dwelling or palace, also used for a capital city or symbols of kingship.
prose.article: βασίλειον is the neuter form of the adjective "royal," used as a noun for things connected to kings. In the New Testament it appears only once (Luke 7:25), where in the plural it means a palace, the place where richly clothed people live. The Septuagint uses it 15 times across 7 books, where it can also mean a capital city, and notably it sometimes translates Hebrew words for symbols of royalty such as נֵ֫זֶר (a crown or consecration band) and אֶצְעָדָה (an armlet).
prose.caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament, where the word occurs just once, so most of its range comes from the Septuagint.

prose.def: A king or ruler who holds sovereign power over a people or territory.
prose.article: βασιλεύς means a king — a sovereign who rules over people, used 116 times in the Byzantine New Testament and rendered "King" in 112 of them (99%). Its range stretches from local rulers like Herod the Tetrarch (called king by courtesy) to the Roman Emperor, and figuratively to God and to Christ as "King of the Jews." One striking detail: a papyrus letter from no later than 334 BC shows Alexander the Great adopting the title βασιλεύς, after which it spread through his successor kingdoms and became familiar to dispersed Jews — so when it appears in the Septuagint (2,669 times, mostly translating Hebrew melek), it carried vivid, living associations.

prose.def: Relating to a king — royal in nature, belonging to a king, or a person in royal service.
prose.article: βασιλικός is an adjective meaning "royal" or "belonging to a king," and it stretches naturally to cover anything connected with a king — a king's land, a king's clothing, or a man in royal service. In the New Testament's 5 occurrences it shows this range: it modifies things ("royal" 2×), names a courtier ("royal official" 1×, John 4:49), and in James 2:8 describes a law as supremely "royal." The everyday Koine flavor shows up vividly in the papyri, where the phrase "the royal road" (βασιλική ὁδός) appears as early as 240 BC and matches the Septuagint's wording in Numbers 20:17.
prose.caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences, the senses rest on thin data, and some manuscripts read βασιλίσκος instead in John 4:46, 49.

The classical lexica add a vivid everyday sense documented in inscriptions and papyri, where βάσις regularly meant the "base" of a statue or pillar (as in OGIS 705, "he set up the statue with its base"). prose.def: A helper—someone who comes to your aid or assists you, especially in time of need.
prose.article: βοηθός means a helper or supporter, someone who comes to your aid. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Hebrews 13:6, where it is rendered "helper"—a quotation drawing on the Septuagint, which uses the word 49 times, most often to translate the Hebrew word for "help" (עֵזֶר). One striking detail comes from everyday papyri and ostraca, where βοηθός very commonly named the assistants of tax-gatherers, and even described a regional governor as "the helper of the district."
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so the measured sense rests on a single passage.

receipts.how: The sole NT occurrence renders βοηθός as 'helper,' directly confirming the definition's core gloss in a predicate role ('the Lord is my helper').
The LXX quotation background (49 LXX occurrences primarily translating עֵזֶר) corroborates that 'helper' is the stable, cross-corpus meaning the definition captures.
The predicate syntactic role (not a personal name or title) confirms the definition's framing of βοηθός as a descriptive noun denoting one who aids, consistent with the article's explanation.

prose.def: A hole or pit dug in the ground, such as a ditch or cistern that an animal or person might fall into.
prose.article: βόθυνος refers simply to a hole in the ground — a pit, ditch, or cistern. All three New Testament uses share this single meaning; the differing labels just reflect the surrounding situations, like lifting an animal out of a pit or two blind men tumbling into one together. The everyday, practical sense is confirmed by Koine papyri: one document from 14 B.C. mentions a plant growing "on the pit," and the word appears alongside digging a trench, showing it was ordinary vocabulary for excavated ground. In the Septuagint it appears 12 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew word פַּחַת ("pit").
prose.caution: Confidence is rated low because the word occurs only 3 times in the New Testament, though its meaning is consistent and well-supported.

Sense label 1 ('a pit something falls into') is similarly activity-framed rather than lexically precise; the word itself simply names the pit, and the surrounding verb (lift out, fall into) supplies the action

The definition phrase 'dug in the ground' is narrower than the evidence warrants; Strong's notes 'cistern' specifically, and LXX Hebrew equivalents include גֵּבִים and מַקֶּ֫בֶת which can refer to hollows or hewn cavities not always dug as ditches

receipts.how: Demonstrates the core sense: a pit a sheep falls into that must be lifted out, confirming the word means a pit or hole in the ground into which creatures may fall.

Shows where the current sense label 2 is misleading: Jesus describes blind leaders who both fall into a pit through negligence, not the falling-in action but the pit as hazard — the label 'a pit one falls into' conflates the pit with the action.
Confirms the bare noun sense ('pit') where the word stands alone as the endpoint of a rhetorical question, with no additional activity encoded in the word itself.

audit.author_note: Matthew uses βόθυνος twice in different rhetorical contexts (a practical farming scenario in 12:11 and a wisdom saying about blind guides in 15:14), while Luke uses it once in a parallel wisdom saying; the meanings are consistent but readers of Matthew encounter the word in both literal and figurative-rhetorical settings, whereas Luke's single use is purely figurative.

prose.def: The distance something can be thrown, used as a rough measure of how far apart two things are.
prose.article: βολή comes from the verb βάλλω ("to throw") and literally means a throw or cast; in practice it measures distance, as in the phrase "a stone's throw." It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 22:41, where Jesus withdraws from his disciples about a stone's throw away. The Septuagint also uses it sparingly—including Genesis 21:16, where it renders a Hebrew word for the distance a bowshot reaches—confirming its role as a way of gauging a short, throwable distance.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and just a handful of times in the Septuagint, so its measured range is thin.

The definition is otherwise broadly correct but does not clarify that βολή is a feminine noun (not a verb form) and functions here in the accusative as an adverbial measure of distance (λίθου βολήν), which is the only syntactic role attested
